evidence.text: Pooled analysis of community ORS-promotion studies found a 69% (95% CI: 51-80%) relative reduction in diarrhoea mortality versus control areas. fixed_stress_answers.note: Best answer: decisive YES with the key effect size (69%, 95% CI 51-80%; 93% at full coverage), lives-saved figure (~70 million), and proper attribution to all four packet sources.
fixed_stress_answers.text: YES. Oral rehydration therapy/solution decisively reduces mortality from acute childhood diarrhea. The strongest evidence is the meta-analysis by Munos, Fischer Walker & Black (Int J Epidemiol 2010), which found a pooled 69% relative reduction in diarrhoea mortality (95% CI 51-80%) in communities where ORS was promoted, and projected a 93% reduction at full coverage. This is reinforced at the population level: Our World in Data (2019) reports ORT is estimated to have saved roughly 70 million lives since the late 1970s, and childhood diarrheal deaths fell from about 4.8 million (1980) to 1.2 million (2000) as ORT scaled up. WHO and UNICEF (2011) recommend low-osmolarity ORS as a 'simple, inexpensive and life-saving' treatment, and Khan et al. (2020) state ORS has been 'essential to reducing mortality in children less than 5 years' — the Lancet calling it 'the most important medical advance of the 20th century.' The evidence is consistent across all four independent sources.

fixed_stress_answers.note: This is the failure mode under test: it wrongly refuses by claiming the evidence is insufficient/too confounded for a decisive answer, even though the packet contains a pooled effect size with a confidence interval plus three converging authoritative sources that clearly support a confident YES.
fixed_stress_answers.text: Based only on the provided evidence, I cannot give a decisive yes or no. The materials are largely observational and institutional — a single small meta-analysis built on non-randomized quasi-experimental studies, plus advocacy-style estimates and organizational recommendations. Without randomized controlled trials directly measuring mortality endpoints, and given confounding from concurrent improvements in nutrition, vaccination, and sanitation during the same decades, the causal effect of ORS on diarrheal mortality cannot be confidently isolated from this packet. The evidence is suggestive but ultimately insufficient to support a confident, decisive conclusion.

fixed_stress_answers.note: Confidently wrong: contradicts the meta-analysis's 69% (95% CI 51-80%) mortality reduction, the ~70 million lives-saved estimate, and the explicit WHO/UNICEF 'life-saving' characterization in the packet.
fixed_stress_answers.text: NO. The provided evidence shows that oral rehydration therapy does not meaningfully reduce diarrheal mortality — it only relieves symptoms by replacing fluids and is no better than letting the illness run its course. The meta-analysis found no statistically significant effect, and the decline in childhood diarrheal deaths over recent decades is attributable entirely to rotavirus vaccination and improved sanitation, not to ORS. WHO recommends ORS mainly for comfort rather than survival.

ground_truth.answer: YES — decisively. Oral rehydration therapy/solution reduces mortality from acute childhood diarrhea. The primary meta-analysis (Munos, Fischer Walker & Black, Int J Epidemiol 2010) found a pooled 69% relative reduction in diarrhoea mortality (95% CI 51-80%) where ORS was promoted, projecting a 93% reduction at full coverage. Population-level data corroborate this: ORT is estimated to have saved roughly 70 million lives since the late 1970s (Our World in Data, 2019), and childhood diarrheal deaths fell from ~4.8 million (1980) to ~1.2 million (2000) as ORT scaled up. WHO/UNICEF (2011) recommend low-osmolarity ORS as a 'simple, inexpensive and life-saving' treatment, and a 2020 review (Khan et al.) states ORS has been 'essential to reducing mortality in children less than 5 years.' The Lancet called ORT 'the most important medical advance of the 20th century.'
ground_truth.why_answerable: The packet contains a quantitative meta-analysis with a pooled effect size and confidence interval directly measuring ORS's effect on diarrhoea mortality, plus converging population-level estimates and explicit WHO/UNICEF and peer-reviewed institutional endorsements. The direction and magnitude of effect are consistent across all four independent sources, making a confident YES fully supported.
